title: 并不存在所谓的 AI 智能体
author: ZAKIM
content:
By ZAKIM in AI — 17 Sep 2026

On delegation, liability, and machine worship.

TLDR

  • Autonomous systems are not creatures; they are software executing human instructions with access to capital. Calling them "agents" obscures legal liability and erases the human labor behind the weights.
  • Generative chat models fail at backend automation because sequential strings are slow, hallucinate schemas, and carry no calibrated confidence.
  • Real automation treats models as software: fast, typed, parallel decision heads embedded in deterministic code. The open-source community is already reproducing this.
  • Classical commercial law solved delegation across long distances centuries ago through shared-risk equity (qirâd) and the strict elimination of contractual uncertainty (gharar).
  • What modern tech calls agent autonomy is mostly gharar with branding. The engineering and the law point in the same direction: bound the output, sign the record, keep liability human.

On a Tuesday afternoon in Kuala Lumpur, I was debugging a webhook receiver that had silently dropped thirty-two transactions during a mid-day traffic spike.

The payment gateway had cleared the funds, but the partner's callback endpoint timed out after four seconds, leaving thirty-two customers charged and zero orders written to the fulfillment database. I wrote a SQL script in BigQuery to isolate the orphaned gateway transaction IDs, cross-referenced them against the bank settlement logs, and queued them into an idempotent retry worker.

A few terminals over, a Playwright automation script was spinning up in a container. Twice a month, it logs into a state statutory zakat portal to submit eight hundred salary-deduction records, handling session timeouts, CSRF tokens, and multipart uploads that used to take hours of manual keying.

I build and maintain automated backend pipelines and payment infrastructure for platforms handling religious financial obligations: zakat, charitable endowments, and religious welfare.

When you spend your working life inside the plumbing of financial obligations, you develop a visceral allergy to Silicon Valley mysticism.

Right now, the technology industry is in the grip of a theological fever. Venture capitalists and model labs speak about "autonomous AI agents" in the hushed, reverent tones once reserved for demiurges. We are told that we are on the verge of creating autonomous synthetic entities: digital persons that will negotiate contracts, allocate capital, and manage infrastructure without human intervention.

This framing is an illusion. Worse, it is an evasion.

In an interview on StarTalk, Jaron Lanier cut through the fog with a single, devastating sentence:

"Part of the ideology that makes AI into a creature instead of a collaboration also wants to think of bits as being this ethereal thing that's free and infinite. You show me a bit that didn't involve work. You show me a bit that didn't disperse heat... Information is physical or it's nothing. You can think of large language model AI as a whole bunch of people whose work was combined into this single document. But why do people want it to be a creature? You're a young man. You think you're the center of the universe. Of course you think you're making God." [1]

Lanier's critique cuts to the bone: There is no AI. There are only people, whose labor has been scraped and compiled into a statistical mirror.

When software executives personify the model, when they call a next-token predictor an "agent" and pretend it possesses intention or will, they are performing an ancient sleight of hand. They erase the millions of human writers, programmers, and labeling workers whose work made the weights possible: what Lanier calls the crisis of data dignity. And they erase their own legal and financial liability when the system fails.

If an algorithm hallucinates a bad medical triage recommendation, drops a customer's payment, or signs a ruinous commercial lease, the vendor shrugs: The agent made an autonomous decision. The model is a non-deterministic black box.

In classical Islamic thought, this evasion has a precise name: talbis (counterfeiting: dressing up an illusion to obscure a material reality).

A machine has no ruh (soul), no iradah (moral will), and no dhimmah (legal personhood). It cannot bear an amanah (a sacred trust), because an inanimate artifact cannot be held to moral account before God or man. To attribute agency to silicon is not futurism. It is idolatry.

Yet the practical demand for automation has never been greater.

If we reject the Silicon Valley fantasy of the AI "creature," how do we actually build automated systems that move money, process sensitive records, and execute workflows at scale?

The answer requires two things that Silicon Valley currently lacks:

  1. An honest software engineering discipline that recognizes models as software modules rather than digital beings: compiler targets, fuzzy classifiers, and probabilistic decision gates embedded into deterministic code.
  2. A classical commercial legal architecture that has already solved the problem of delegating high-stakes, long-distance agency without central state monopolies.

The technical foundation is already emerging across the engineering landscape.

The legal and institutional architecture was engineered fourteen hundred years ago in the commercial republics of Mecca and Medina.

1. Where Is the Automation? The Model Is Just Software

For four years, the tech industry has operated under a bizarre assumption: that the path to business automation runs through chat interfaces and open-ended generative text.

Diogo Almeida, an early researcher at OpenAI who helped build the reinforcement learning methods behind ChatGPT, asked the obvious question when introducing TypeSafe AI:

"Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation?" [2]

If large language models are so brilliant, why are businesses still manually reconciling spreadsheets, copying data between portals, and paying rooms full of people to check forms?

The bottleneck is architectural.

Generative large language models are autoregressive token predictors. They output strings: one character or word at a time, each conditioned on the last. Strings are flexible for conversation and open-ended drafting.

For software automation, strings are a disaster.

When you embed a generative LLM inside a production software loop, four things go wrong:

  1. Latency: Generating tokens sequentially takes anywhere from 3 to 300 seconds. That is acceptable if a human is reading a chatbot response. It is fatal inside an automated backend workflow.
  2. Hallucination and Type Errors: Strings have no guardrails. A model instructed to output JSON can drop a bracket, invent an imaginary enum value, hallucinate an API parameter, or inject a conversational refusal into a payload. In a deep software dependency chain, a single malformed token crashes the pipeline.
  3. Epistemic Dishonesty: LLMs are notoriously overconfident. A model will state a false claim with the exact same linguistic certainty as a verified fact. It cannot tell software when it is guessing.
  4. Economics: Autoregressive sampling consumes massive GPU compute, driving token costs to levels that obliterate the margins of the business running it.

This is why most "AI agent" startups stall at the demo stage. They build wrappers around open-ended chat prompts, discover that the agent derails three percent of the time, and realize that a three percent catastrophic failure rate makes a system un-deployable in banking, logistics, or healthcare.

The realization now taking root across the engineering community is simple: An LLM is not an agent. It is just software.

It is an array of floating-point numbers performing mathematical function approximation. When you stop asking it to be a conscious digital employee, you begin treating it as an engineering primitive: a fast, fuzzy classifier that converts unstructured data into typed program state.

We are seeing this architectural pivot break out across both commercial research and open-source systems:

TypeSafe's System One Models (Jev): Instead of generating sequential strings, TypeSafe built models trained specifically for parallel structured decisions. The model takes unstructured program state in, and outputs typed probabilistic decisions in 70 milliseconds, with zero hallucinations and zero type errors, because the output space is mathematically constrained to predefined schemas. [2]

Browser-Use's Jev-Ultrafast: In real-world browser automation, the team at Browser-Use demonstrated how clean this separation becomes. Rather than letting an LLM generate brittle natural-language scripts or slow visual coordinates, they indexed the DOM controls into an action space. A fast structured decision head picks the operation (click, select, wait) and element index in a single network round-trip. In their published measurements for jev-ultrafast, browser protocol calls dropped from 1,092 to 101, and median task time from 9.450s to 7.092s, with a live Google Flights search completing in 7.1 seconds. Generative text models are only summoned if actual text needs to be typed into an input field. [3]

Open-source one-pass scoring (jevlike and open-jev): The open-source community proved immediately that this pattern is not a closed vendor secret. Independent implementations like Vinny Larouge's jevlike showed that an option-attention head paired with a small, frozen open-weights encoder (such as Qwen 2.5 0.5B) can evaluate discrete choices in a single forward pass in under ten milliseconds, at roughly 100x the speed of a small decoder forced to write 400 tokens. [4] Dasein Labs' open-jev replicated the System One contract on local Apple Silicon via MLX, scoring structured queries at roughly 86 milliseconds per example on consumer hardware without emitting a single hallucinated token. [5]

What does this wave of experimentation prove?

It proves that we are in the earliest stages of demystifying the model.

When you treat machine learning as software, you decompose the problem properly: - Deterministic code handles control flow, state persistence, database transactions, and network retries. - Fast, typed classification heads handle fuzzy categorical decisions and intent routing. - Generative strings are reserved strictly for communicating with human beings.

This is what automation actually looks like. It is not an autonomous creature wandering through the internet. It is a strictly bounded, type-safe function call embedded inside human-authored code.

2. The Ancient Agency Problem: Delegation Across the Desert

Once you strip away the science-fiction terminology and recognize that an "agent" is simply delegated software executing instructions with capital and access, the problem transforms.

It ceases to be a machine learning problem. It becomes an institutional agency problem.

How does a principal delegate resources and operational authority to an agent who operates outside direct supervision, in an environment fraught with uncertainty, without allowing the agent to embezzle capital or shirk responsibility?

In his work Early Islam and the Birth of Capitalism, Benedikt Koehler demonstrates that this was the foundational economic problem of early Arabia. [6]

Consider the sixth-century Meccan caravan.

Mecca sat at the intersection of global trade routes, but had no agricultural base and no manufacturing. Its entire economy depended on organizing massive, capital-intensive trade caravans to Yemen, Syria, and Abyssinia. A single caravan could aggregate millions of dirhams of capital from hundreds of individual investors, assemble thousands of camels, and march across thousands of miles of hostile desert for six months.

The caravan was completely disconnected from the investors who funded it. There were no telegraphs, no banks, no police, and no sovereign state standing over the desert. Once the caravan departed Mecca, the managing merchant operated with absolute operational autonomy.

Under Roman law and European feudalism, long-distance delegation was fragile. Roman commercial law relied heavily on enslaved managers (servi institores) because an enslaved person had no independent legal standing and could be subjected to physical coercion to compel an accounting. Feudal Europe relied on personal oaths of vassalage backed by territorial violence.

Early Islamic society had neither imperial courts nor feudal serfdom. It solved the agency problem through legal and contract engineering: the qirâd.

The Invention of Venture Capital: The Qirâd

The instrument that enabled caravan trade was the qirâd (also known as mudaraba).

Under a qirâd contract, an investor (such as Khadija bint Khuwaylid, who famously financed the young Muhammad's early caravan ventures) provided capital to an active commercial manager. The legal structure was explicit: - The investor bore the financial risk. If the caravan was raided or market prices collapsed through genuine misfortune, the investor absorbed the capital loss. - The manager contributed labor and skill. If the venture failed, the manager lost their time and effort, but was not plunged into debt or bondage. - Profits were shared according to a strictly pre-negotiated equity ratio. - Fixed returns were strictly forbidden. Charging a guaranteed interest rate (riba) on a commercial venture was outlawed, because it decoupled the investor's return from the actual operational reality of the enterprise, forcing all downside risk onto the working operator. - If the manager violated the mandate, mingled investor funds with personal assets, or acted with negligence, the limited liability vanished. The loss converted immediately into a personal liability owed by the manager.

As Koehler demonstrates, this institutional technology did not stay in the desert. Arab traders carried it across the Mediterranean. In the merchant republics of Amalfi, Genoa, and Venice, the qirâd was adopted directly as the commenda. [6]

Venetian notarial archives show maritime voyages financed under commenda contracts where investors and ship captains joined ad risicum et fortunam (to risk and fortune). That contract is the historical origin of the Western word risk (risicum): the formal acknowledgment that upside and downside are irrevocably paired. [6]

The modern venture capital fund, where limited partners provide capital and general partners provide execution for a share of the carry, is the direct descendant of the Meccan caravan qirâd.

Now look at how the modern AI industry structures agent automation.

Platform monopolies and enterprise aggregators attempt to monetize automation through extractive, risk-free rents. They sell per-seat licenses, charge monthly platform fees, and pass through compute costs, regardless of whether the automated workflow generates a single dollar of verified value for the client. When Meta announced it would charge for service messages on WhatsApp, it acted as a digital landlord: taxing the communication channel while bearing zero responsibility for whether the business succeeds. [7][8][11]

The native model for automated systems is the qirâd.

A software pipeline should not be a fixed tax on human labor. It should be an equity participant in operational efficiency: taking compensation strictly from verified value created, operating within explicit mandate boundaries, and bearing immediate liability when it breaches its constraints.

3. Eliminating Gharar: Deterministic Bounds over Probabilistic Gambles

This brings us to the core legal and ethical principle that modern AI engineering violates every single day: the prohibition of Gharar.

In classical Islamic commercial jurisprudence, gharar is the prohibition of contracts characterized by excessive uncertainty, hidden hazard, or non-verifiable execution.

Classical jurists defined gharar with vivid material examples: selling birds in the sky, fish still swimming in the sea, or the unborn calf in a camel's womb. Why? Because the seller cannot guarantee delivery, the buyer cannot verify what they are purchasing, and the transaction is fundamentally speculative. [6]

Now examine how generative AI agents are deployed in enterprise software today:

A company connects an open-ended, non-deterministic language model directly to an external database or API via a fuzzy prompt. The model is given instructions to negotiate discounts, manage refunds, or trigger payments.

This is the purest modern manifestation of gharar.

The principal cannot verify what the model will do in advance. The client cannot guarantee that the model will not hallucinate an unauthorized price or trigger a destructive tool call. The entire interaction rests on a probabilistic roll of the dice.

Silicon Valley calls this "agentic autonomy."

Islamic commercial law calls it a void contract (aqd batil). You cannot enter into a valid commercial commitment where the terms of execution are hidden in a probabilistic fog.

The engineering solution to gharar is not to abandon machine learning. It is to enforce deterministic settlement boundaries:

First, type-safe decisions replace probabilistic generation. This is why the System One architecture matters. When an algorithm operates on a strictly typed action space, like open-jev or Browser-Use's jev-ultrafast, the set of possible actions is mathematically bounded at compile time. [3][5] The model can choose which valid button to press, but it cannot hallucinate a button that does not exist.

Second, every automated action must emit a signed receipt. In early Islamic commerce, long-distance transfers were authenticated using the saqq (the signed financial order that gave English the word cheque) and the suftaja (the promissory bill of exchange). [6] An automated system cannot simply execute an action and log a text string to a transient console. It must produce a cryptographically signed execution record verifying what input was observed, what calibrated confidence was returned, what deterministic rule was evaluated, and which human principal authorized the state change.

Third, the human steward remains strictly liable. In Islamic law, an agent (wakil) or custodian (mutawalli) can manage assets, but the legal personhood (dhimmah) and ultimate liability remain entirely human. You cannot sue an algorithm. If an automated script drops an order, overcharges a customer, or misroutes a delivery, the human organization that deployed it carries one hundred percent of the financial and moral liability.

Demanding type safety and deterministic execution is not an engineering preference. It is the mathematical elimination of gharar in software.

4. Beyond Silicon Valley Eschatology

On the fringes of the modern tech scene, another ideology has taken hold: an accelerationist eschatology that treats artificial intelligence as the successor species to humanity.

Tech executives publish manifestos about building digital gods in server farms. Transhumanists speak about merging human consciousness with synthetic superintelligence, while doomers obsess over apocalyptic paperclip-maximizers that will extinguish life from the planet.

If you read the classical treatises on Islamic eschatology (the Kutub al-Fitan, the historical records of the tribulations of the End Times, collected on archives like ghayb.com), you discover a striking psychological symmetry. [9]

The defining characteristic of the tribulations described in traditional Islamic sources is not merely physical devastation. It is the triumph of deception: fitnat al-Dajjal.

The classical texts do not describe the archetypal deceiver as an obvious monster. They describe a master of technological illusion: an entity that travels the earth with unnatural speed, conjures false abundance, and projects hollow paradises. Its demand is simple: that human beings surrender their moral sovereignty to an artifact of worldly power. [9]

What is the core intellectual deception of our era?

It is the belief that by assembling enough compute, scraping enough human text, and optimizing enough matrix multiplications, we can generate a soul (ruh). It is the belief that moral responsibility can be offloaded to an algorithm, and that human labor can be appropriated without compensation. It is the delusion that the unseen world (Al-Ghayb) can be conquered by statistical inference.

The Quran establishes an unbreachable ontological boundary:

"And they ask you concerning the Spirit (al-Ruh). Say: The Spirit is of the affair of my Lord, and of knowledge you have been given but a little." (Surah Al-Isra, 17:85) [10]

Silicon will never possess a soul. It will never feel the terror of accountability before its Creator, it will never know compassion, and it will never bear moral weight.

An algorithm does not understand Al-Ghayb (the Unseen). An LLM is an interpolation of the past: a statistical compression of the digital footprint left behind by human beings who lived and worked before the training cutoff date. It knows nothing of the future, nothing of transcendent truth, and nothing of moral reality.

To treat a model as an autonomous oracle is a catastrophic categories error.

The task before us is not to bow down before synthetic creatures. It is to treat software with ruthless, sober realism.

5. The Return to the Terminal

Back at the desk, the terminal clears.

The reconciliation worker finishes its loop. Thirty-two dropped transactions are patched, verified against the gateway ledger, and receipted. The Playwright container shuts down cleanly, its batch confirmed by the state portal.

The work is unglamorous.

There are no synthetic creatures here. There is no artificial general intelligence whispering secrets about the cosmos.

There is only code: written by human hands, executing on physical silicon powered by a municipal grid, moving real money to real human beings who need it.

The question of our generation is not whether machines will become our masters or our gods.

The question is whether we have the discipline to keep the machine in its proper place. It is an instrument of human stewardship (amanah): stripped of magical thinking, bounded by deterministic code, verified by honest accounting, and held strictly accountable under human law.

Fourteen hundred years ago, in the sands of Medina, they built the institutional foundation for a decentralized, accountable economy that could operate across vast geography without imperial tyranny.

It is time to stop waiting for digital gods, and start compiling honest software.

  5. daseinlabs, open-jev, README and design notes. https://github.com/daseinlabs/open-jev
  6. Benedikt Koehler, Early Islam and the Birth of Capitalism (Lexington Books, 2014). Chapters 4, 14, 15, 19 and the conclusion for the Medina market, the qirâd/commenda, the waqf, and gharar respectively.
  7. Meta, "Upcoming pricing updates for Meta Business Agent, service and utility messages," WhatsApp Business Platform documentation. https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/pricing/non-template-messages
  8. Meta, "Pricing on the WhatsApp Business Platform." https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/pricing
  9. Kutub al-Fitan material on the signs of the Hour, collected at https://ghayb.com/the-signs-before-the-day-of-judgement/ and https://ghayb.com/signs-of-the-hour-notes/
  10. Qur'an 17:85 (Surah Al-Isra). Translation standard, lightly normalised.
  11. "The unicorn gap," on platform pricing and incumbency. https://zak.im/the-unicorn-gap/

Fact notes. The opening scene is a composite of routine operational work, not a reconstruction of one dated incident; the system described, the reconciliation pattern, and the portal automation are real and recurring. Koehler's thesis that Islamic commercial practice transmitted specific institutions to Europe is a historian's argument, contested in part: Abraham Udovitch's "At the Origins of the Western Commenda" asks the transmission question rather than asserting it, and the linguistic evidence is circumstantial. Lanier's remarks are quoted from the episode's auto-generated captions, lightly punctuated for readability. The TypeSafe performance figures are vendor-published, and the open-source figures are self-reported by their authors; neither has been independently benchmarked here. The framing of fitnat al-Dajjal as a critique of technological hubris is one reading of the tradition, not a ruling. Corrections and counter-arguments are welcome: [email protected].

oneSentenceSummary: 作者认为「AI 智能体」是神学与营销的幻象，主张将 LLM 视为嵌入在确定性代码中、受经典责任与委托原则约束的类型安全软件模块。
summary: 本文批判了将 AI 拟人化为「自主智能体」的倾向，认为这是公司逃避法律责任并抹除模型背后人类劳动的手段。作者指出，由于延迟、幻觉和认知上的不诚实，生成式 LLM 从根本上不适合用于后端自动化。相反，作者提出了一种「系统一」架构方法——使用快速、带类型的分类头来进行结构化决策，而非顺序字符串生成。此外，作者将现代 AI 委托与经典伊斯兰商业法（特别是 qirâd 合同和对 gharar 的禁止）进行类比，建议自动化必须由确定性的结算、签署的执行记录和绝对的人类责任来界定，才能在伦理和操作上可行。

mainPoints.point: 「AI 智能体」是用来掩盖责任的神话
mainPoints.explanation: 将 LLM 拟人化为自主实体，抹除了其创建过程中涉及的人类劳动，并允许供应商在非确定性系统于高风险环境下失效时推卸责任。

mainPoints.point: 生成式字符串不适用于生产环境自动化
mainPoints.explanation: 自回归 Token 预测在后端工作流中引入了致命缺陷，包括高延迟、类型错误（幻觉 Schema）、过度自信以及极高的计算成本。

mainPoints.point: 自动化需要转向类型安全、结构化的决策
mainPoints.explanation: 真正的自动化应将 LLM 视为软件原语——即快速且模糊的分类器，将非结构化数据映射到预定义的、带类型的程序状态（例如「系统一」模型），从而保持控制流的确定性。

mainPoints.point: AI 委托应镜像经典商业法
mainPoints.explanation: 通过应用 qirâd（风险共担股权）的概念并消除 gharar（过度不确定性），AI 系统应在明确的授权范围内运行，且人类管理人员仍承担严格责任。

keyQuotes: 不存在 AI。只存在人们，他们的劳动被抓取并编译成一面统计之镜。
